reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: Caused by heterozygous mutations in HNF1A with autosomal dominant inheritance and a strong multigenerational history of young-onset diabetes
Typically presents in adolescence or young adulthood with progressive hyperglycaemia rather than the stable elevation seen in GCK-MODY
A hallmark is marked sensitivity to sulfonylureas, which are often the treatment of choice and can allow insulin to be stopped
A low renal threshold for glucose can produce glycosuria at near-normal plasma glucose levels, an early diagnostic clue
Patients are typically lean and pancreatic autoantibody negative, distinguishing them from type 1 diabetes
Microvascular complications can develop over time, so glycaemic control and surveillance remain important
High-sensitivity C-reactive protein tends to be low, which can support the diagnosis alongside genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: HNF1A is a transcription factor essential for normal beta-cell development and function, regulating genes involved in glucose sensing and insulin secretion. Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations cause a progressive decline in insulin secretory capacity, so hyperglycaemia worsens over time in contrast to the stable defect of GCK-MODY. The transcription factor also governs renal glucose reabsorption, explaining the characteristically low renal threshold. The residual beta-cell KATP channel responsiveness underlies the pronounced clinical sensitivity to sulfonylureas.
additionalDifferentials: Type 2 diabetes mellitus in a young lean adult
HNF4A-MODY, which has an overlapping phenotype
additionalInvestigations: Fasting glucose and HbA1c documenting progressive hyperglycaemia
Molecular genetic testing of HNF1A to confirm the diagnosis
Negative pancreatic autoantibodies to exclude type 1 diabetes
Urinalysis or paired glucose testing demonstrating a low renal glucose threshold
High-sensitivity C-reactive protein as a supportive biomarker where available
redFlags: Ketoacidosis or rapid decompensation, which is atypical and warrants reassessment
Progressive rise in glycaemia despite therapy, indicating declining beta-cell reserve
Development of microvascular complications requiring intensified surveillance
Severe hypoglycaemia after starting sulfonylureas because of exaggerated drug sensitivity
reference.prognosis: With correct diagnosis many patients achieve good control on low-dose sulfonylureas for years, but insulin secretion declines progressively and microvascular complications can occur, so long-term monitoring is required.
pitfalls: Defaulting to insulin when a trial of sulfonylurea would be more appropriate and effective
Misdiagnosing the condition as type 1 diabetes because of young age at onset
Overlooking the family history that signals a dominant monogenic cause
Failing to anticipate exaggerated sulfonylurea sensitivity and consequent hypoglycaemia
management: Treat first-line with low-dose sulfonylureas, harnessing the marked sulfonylurea sensitivity of HNF1A-MODY, which often lets insulin be discontinued
Titrate the sulfonylurea cautiously from a low starting dose to avoid hypoglycaemia
Escalate to additional oral agents or insulin as insulin secretory capacity declines progressively
Sustain glycaemic control and undertake regular surveillance for microvascular and macrovascular complications
Coordinate pregnancy care with specialists, monitoring maternal glucose
Offer genetic counselling and cascade testing of relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance
Refer to endocrinology and clinical genetics for genetic confirmation and long-term follow-up
